The history of the Roman Empire is a vast and complex topic, spanning over 12 centuries. It began in 753 BC, when the city of Rome was founded by Romulus and Remus, two legendary brothers who are said to have been raised by a she-wolf. The early Roman Kingdom was ruled by a series of seven kings, with Romulus being the first. This period, known as the Roman Kingdom, lasted from 753 BC to 509 BC, and was characterized by the development of Roman institutions, laws, and architecture.

During this time, the Romans were heavily influenced by the Etruscan civilization, which had a significant impact on the development of Roman art, architecture, and engineering. The Romans also began to expand their territory, conquering the surrounding regions of Latium and eventually, the entire Italian peninsula. The last king of Rome, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in 509 BC, marking the end of the Roman Kingdom and the beginning of the Roman Republic.

The Roman Republic, which lasted from 509 BC to 27 BC, was a period of significant expansion and growth for the Romans. They developed a system of governance based on representative democracy, with power held by the Senate and the Assemblies. The Romans also developed a powerful military, which allowed them to conquer much of Italy, as well as parts of North Africa, Spain, and Gaul (modern-day France). Key figures such as Julius Caesar, Pompey, and Cicero played important roles in shaping the Roman Republic, with Caesar's rise to power ultimately leading to the end of the Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire.
